title: Does Deterministic Generate–Validate–Repair Reduce Unsafe LLM‑Generated Network Changes? A Confirmatory Paired Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a sealed paired confirmatory study (n = 200 intent→configuration tasks) to test whether a deterministic generate–validate–repair (GVR) pipeline that consults a deterministic NetOps validator reduces validator‑detected unsafe or semantically incorrect network changes relative to an LLM‑only generation pipeline. The run used a single hosted model (gpt‑5‑mini) under adapter‑enforced shared‑initial generation semantics and a primary deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5). Execution completed all planned pairs (200 complete pairs) consuming 200 model calls (one shared initial generation per task); no repair calls were issued because every initial candidate passed the validator. Paired contingency: n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0; estimate = 0.0; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; 95% bootstrap percentile CI = [0.0, 0.0] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). Because baseline validator‑detected unsafe incidence was 0% on this task bank, the preregistered ≥50% relative‑reduction hypothesis could not be meaningfully evaluated. We report the sealed design, precise execution accounting, an independent Mininet 10% holdout that produced zero validator–emulator disagreements, and an artifact‑grounded discussion of operational implications and threats to validity (preregistration id: cnsms2026‑gvr‑effectiveness‑02).

sections.introduction: Automating intent→configuration translation with large language models (LLMs) promises operational productivity gains for network operations (NetOps) but entails the risk of generating incorrect or unsafe configuration changes that can cause outages or policy violations. Prior work therefore advocates grounding and deterministic validation—often organized as generate–validate–repair (GVR) loops—to detect and correct unsafe candidates before they are applied. However, the operational benefit of automated repair depends on: baseline prevalence of validator‑detectable failures for the chosen generator/prompting policy; validator coverage and fidelity; and the available repair budget and its effectiveness. We preregistered a narrowly scoped confirmatory question to probe a concrete operational claim: Does an automated, deterministic GVR pipeline that consults a deterministic NetOps validator materially reduce validator‑detected unsafe or semantically incorrect network changes relative to an LLM‑only generation pipeline on a curated 200‑task intent→configuration bank? The study used a paired design that fixes the generator output per task and isolates the marginal effect of invoking the validator and, if necessary, issuing a single automated repair call on that identical candidate.
sections.related_work: LLM outputs commonly exhibit factual errors and hallucinations across domains; mitigation patterns include retrieval grounding, deterministic checkers, and verifier‑assisted repair. Surveys of LLM applications and AIOps characterize prompt sensitivity, non‑determinism, and the need for verification layers. In NetOps, a body of prototypes shows feasibility for intent→configuration generation but lacks instrumented studies that quantify operational failure rates under realistic generation policies. Architectural proposals advocate binding LLMs to deterministic validators (Batfish‑style checkers) and using guarded agent patterns; red‑team audits highlight configuration‑level brittleness and tool‑description injection vectors that can change safety outcomes. Our work differs by preregistering a confirmatory paired estimand, executing the sealed experiment, and publishing a compact, artifact‑grounded account of why the trial produced a null marginal effect under the tested design choices. Representative verified sources supporting these background points are cited in the bibliography and include recent surveys and NetOps prototype evaluations.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and inferential plan. We preregistered the study as cnsms2026‑gvr‑effectiveness‑02 with a paired design (n = 200 tasks), one deterministic shared initial generation per task, and a repair budget of at most one automated repair call per task. The primary estimand was the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline; the primary test was an exact two‑sided McNemar test (α = 0.05). Confidence intervals were computed via the bootstrap percentile method with 10,000 resamples (bootstrap_seed = 1729). Planning assumed a baseline unsafe incidence ≈30% and targeted a 50% relative reduction; these assumptions only motivated sample size. The confirmatory analysis was executed by a deterministic paired binary analysis routine as preregistered.

Task bank, validator, and holdout. The benchmark was a curated, machine‑checkable intent→configuration bank of 200 tasks across four topology clusters (enterprise, campus, datacenter, edge; 50 tasks each). Each task encodes initial and expected final states, workflow constraints (make‑before‑break, must_be_down_for_fields, group minima), and a required_sequence; the primary deterministic checker enforces syntax and intent/constraint checks and emits structured diagnostics (valid flag, violation codes, parsed_command_count, required_command_count). A Mininet‑based data‑plane emulator served as a secondary disagreement detector on a randomized 10% holdout (20 tasks) to detect validator–emulator mismatches; that preregistered check produced zero disagreement flags in this run. All experiment artifacts (model calls, validator traces, logs, and analysis outputs) are archived in the execution bundle for external inspection.

Adapter semantics and determinism reconciliation. The adapter used (hosted_netops_gvr_v1) enforced shared_initial generation semantics: for each task a single deterministic initial candidate was produced and reused for both baseline and guarded conditions. This design isolates the marginal effect of invoking the validator and issuing at most one repair on the identical generator output. Regarding runtime sampling: the archived model configuration declares the requested model as gpt‑5‑mini and explicitly records the model configuration temperature field as unset (null) in the stored configuration. Determinism for the confirmatory contrast was therefore not achieved by a recorded explicit model temperature parameter alone but by adapter enforcement of a single shared invocation per task; provider/audit accounting fields confirm hosted_model_call counts consistent with that enforcement. We state this explicitly to resolve an ambiguity observed during review: determinism was enforced at the adapter/orchestration level (shared_initial invocation semantics), and adapter/provider audit artifacts demonstrate single invocations per task rather than relying on a model parameter alone.

Repair policy, budgeting, and contamination plan. When the primary validator reported violations the adapter would issue at most one automated repair prompt to the same LLM; any repaired candidate would be re‑validated by the deterministic checker. The execution contract limited maximum model calls to 400 (200 initial + up to 200 repairs); the adapter enforced this cap. The contamination plan prescribed excluding pairs where the primary validator and the Mininet emulator disagreed; in that case a conservative exclusion was applied in the primary analysis and deterministic sensitivity analyses were planned. All exclusion and missingness rules were preregistered and deterministic.

Statistical procedures and reproducibility parameters. The primary confirmatory test was the exact McNemar two‑sided test on the 2×2 paired table (n11, n10, n01, n00). Bootstrap percentile CIs used 10,000 resamples with seed 1729. Task ordering and other randomized elements had fixed seeds recorded in the task manifest entries; the run archive contains the analysis log documenting these parameters. We note a reproducibility limitation: the explicit labeled randomized selection seed for the Mininet 10% holdout selection is absent from the labeled artifact set, which prevents exact deterministic reconstruction of the drawn holdout even though the contamination summary reports zero disagreements.
sections.results:
Execution accounting. The run completed all planned episodes: completed_episode_count = 400 (shared initial generation reused across baseline and guarded conditions), complete_pair_count = 200, model_calls_used = 200 (one shared initial generation per task), maximum_model_calls = 400, and repair_calls_used = 0. Adapter/provider audit accounting confirms hosted_model_call_event_count = 200 and stage counts consistent with a single shared initial invocation per task.

Validator outcomes and paired contingency. Every initial candidate passed the primary deterministic validator: baseline_success_count = 200/200 and guarded_success_count = 200/200. The paired contingency table is n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. The observed paired difference estimate = 0.0. The prespecified exact McNemar two‑sided test yields p = 1.0. Bootstrap percentile confidence intervals (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) produce a 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0]. Under the preregistered estimand the preregistered ≥50% relative‑reduction hypothesis cannot be evaluated on this sample because baseline validator failures were absent.

Repair and secondary outcomes. Because no validator failures were observed the repair branch was never invoked and the preregistered secondary estimands (average repair iterations per repaired task, GVR‑introduced failure rate, model‑call cost per successful repair) have no empirical data from this run. The Mininet 10% holdout produced zero validator–emulator disagreements in the executed sample; however, as noted, the explicit holdout selection seed is not available among the labeled artifacts, which constrains exact reproducibility of that holdout draw.

Representative diagnostics. Archived per‑task validator traces show that parsed_command_count equaled required_command_count for representative examples and that validator validation_after.valid flags were true with violation_count = 0, including tasks annotated with nontrivial difficulty patterns ("make_before_break_uplink_switchover", "paired_link_atomic_mtu_change", "rolling_access_vlan_migration"). These diagnostics illustrate that the task bank exercised dependency constraints even when the generator outputs satisfied the machine‑checkable constraints under the chosen generation policy.
sections.discussion:
Conditional interpretation. The confirmatory null outcome (zero baseline validator failures) is an artifact‑grounded result: both baseline and guarded conditions produced validator‑passing configurations for every task under the shared_initial generation policy. The statistical mechanics are straightforward: with zero discordant pairs the exact McNemar p = 1.0 and the bootstrapped 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0]. These numbers do not imply that repair architectures are universally ineffective; rather they demonstrate that GVR’s marginal utility depends on baseline validator failure prevalence and validator coverage for the targeted workload and generation policy.

Why the null occurred. The archived artifacts document several contributing factors: (1) task specifications encoded explicit required_sequences and workflow constraints and the primary validator enforces those constraints—on each task the generator output satisfied the checks; (2) the adapter enforced shared_initial semantics (single invocation per task), removing sampling variance as a pathway to observe alternative failing candidates; and (3) the Mininet holdout (20 tasks) revealed no validator–emulator mismatches in the executed draw. Together these factors created a setting in which there was nothing for the preregistered repair mechanism to correct under the selected design choices.

Methodological tradeoffs and implications. The shared_initial paired design isolates the incremental causal effect of validating/repairing the same generator output, which is valuable for internal validity but cannot capture gains obtainable by re‑sampling the generator (e.g., drawing alternative candidates that repair calls could then correct). For practitioners estimating unconditional operational failure rates, independent per‑condition multi‑sample designs or nonzero temperature sampling better capture unconditional risk. If baseline validator failures are rare in a deployment, investing effort into expanding validator fidelity, adversarial testing, or enabling multi‑sample generation and richer repair budgets may yield larger safety returns than a single‑call repair loop. Conversely, when baseline failures are common, GVR with a suitably sized repair budget can reduce validator‑detected errors.

Validator completeness and emulator corroboration. Deterministic validators provide necessary but not sufficient safety oracles; they codify a check set that can miss device idiosyncrasies. The Mininet holdout is a pragmatic secondary check for validator blind spots; the zero disagreements observed here do not prove coverage across production heterogeneity. We therefore recommend combined programs that scale emulation or testbed checks, instrument adversarial perturbations, and record all random seeds used to draw holdouts to enable exact reproducibility.

Reproducibility and the documented gap. In response to review, we explicitly disclose the missing labeled randomized seed used to select the Mininet 10% holdout in the archived labeled artifacts. This absence prevents bit‑for‑bit reconstruction of that exact holdout draw; it does not alter the reported contamination summary (zero disagreements) but constrains external auditors from deterministically reproducing which tasks were emulated. We treat this as a concrete reproducibility limitation and recommend that future runs include explicit labeled seeds for every randomized selection applied to secondary checks.
sections.conclusion: We preregistered and executed a sealed paired study comparing LLM‑only generation to a deterministic GVR pipeline on 200 NetOps intent→configuration tasks using gpt‑5‑mini and a deterministic NetOps validator. Both pipelines produced validator‑passing configurations for every task (n11 = 200; no discordant pairs), yielding an observed paired difference of 0.0, exact McNemar p = 1.0, and bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0]. Because baseline validator failures were absent, the preregistered ≥50% relative‑reduction hypothesis was not testable on this sample. The artifact‑grounded outcome emphasizes that GVR’s marginal value is workload dependent: when baseline validator‑detectable failures are rare under a specific generator and sampling policy, a single automated repair pass yields no measured marginal benefit for those validator‑detected errors. Future confirmatory studies should target workloads with nontrivial baseline failure rates, expand validator fidelity, record all random seeds used in secondary checks, evaluate multi‑sample and multi‑model policies, and explore multi‑step or human‑in‑the‑loop repair budgets to characterize operational gains. All execution artifacts and analysis outputs are archived under the preregistration id cited above for independent inspection.

Preregistration and freeze: the experimental plan (estimand, sample size n = 200, paired design, stopping rules, max model calls = 400, repair budget = 1 per task, shared‑initial generation semantics) was frozen before any model calls. Deviations and restarts: no post‑preregistration design changes or technical restarts occurred.
limitations: Task‑bank scope: the confirmatory sample used a curated synthetic/public intent→configuration bank (n = 200); results therefore reflect this bank and may not generalize to broader production workloads or adversarial distributions.

Single‑model and shared‑initial setting: only gpt‑5‑mini (hosted) with adapter‑enforced shared‑initial generation was tested; outcomes may differ across model families, independent per‑condition sampling, nonzero temperature sampling, or larger repair budgets.

Validator coverage and oracle limitations: the primary deterministic validator enforces a defined set of syntax/intent checks; validators can fail to capture real device idiosyncrasies, vendor‑specific behaviors, or emergent failure modes detectable only by end‑to‑end deployment.

Adversarial robustness untested: this confirmatory run did not include active adversarial injection or red‑team tool‑description attacks; prior audits indicate such vectors can bypass naive defenses and remain a separate concern.

Reproducibility gap for contamination check: the randomized holdout selection seed for the Mininet contamination check is absent from the labeled artifacts, preventing exact reconstruction of the holdout selection.

Single repair budget: the GVR pipeline allowed at most one automated repair prompt per task; multi‑step repair strategies, different repair budgets, or human‑in‑the‑loop approvals were not exercised here.
